WASHINGTON (CNN) -- House and Senate Democrats reached agreement late Monday on a budget resolution for 2010, which includes key spending priorities for the young Obama administration. The Senate and House could vote on the budget resolution Tuesday. President Obama's budget request is $3.67 trillion. "This budget is a major accomplishment," Senate Budget Committee Chairman Kent Conrad said in a statement. "We are meeting President Obama's goals of reducing our dependence on foreign energy, striving for excellence in education, reforming our health care system, and providing middle-class tax relief." The agreement came as lawmakers were reconciling the House and Senate versions of the budget package. The president's budget request is $3.67 trillion. The full Senate and House are each expected to vote on the fiscal 2010 budget resolution this week. The House vote could come as soon as Tuesday. Budget negotiators have fast-tracked part of the budget process. Major health reform is likely to pass this year, because the special process -- known as budget reconciliation -- won't allow Republicans to filibuster the legislation, as was widely expected. Democrats, who currently control 58 seats in the Senate, will be able to pass it with a simple majority vote, instead of the 60 needed to overcome a filibuster. Separately, conservative Democrats in the House, who have been pushing for a strong statement from leadership on fiscal responsibility in the budget, may have some of their concerns addressed. A Democratic aide told CNN that House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House Majority Whip Steny Hoyer are drafting a letter to Senate leaders "throwing down the gauntlet" to insist that a pay-as-you-go system be followed, which would require new federal spending to be offset with budget cuts or tax increases. President Barack Obama called for the so-called "PAYGO" legislation in his weekend radio address. The budget resolution would limit increases in non-defense discretionary spending to 2.9 percent through 2014, according to Conrad. "While the budget resolution takes important steps in the near-term of cutting the deficit in half by 2012 and by two-thirds by 2014, it is clear that more will be needed to address the long-term fiscal imbalance confronting the nation beyond the five-year budget window," said Conrad. President Obama gathered his Cabinet members last week and challenged them to cut a total of $100 million in the next 90 days. In the context of the federal budget, $100 million in savings is a tiny amount, critics said. It is the equivalent, according to one example, of having a car dealer offer to shave $1 from the cost of a $36,700 vehicle. "Any amount of savings is obviously welcome," Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Kentucky, said at the time. "But ($100 million is) about the average amount we'll spend every single day just covering the interest on the stimulus package that we passed earlier this year." White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs said ordinary Americans would nevertheless appreciate the savings effort. "Only in Washington, D.C., is $100 million dollars not a lot of money. It is where I'm from. It is where I grew up. And I think it is for hundreds of millions of Americans." CNN's Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

President Obama’s budget request totals $3.67 trillion.

The agreement came as lawmakers worked to reconcile the House and Senate versions of the budget package. The full Senate and House are each expected to vote on the fiscal 2010 budget resolution this week, with the House vote possible as soon as Tuesday.

Budget negotiators have accelerated part of the budget process. Major health care reform is likely to pass this year because the special procedure known as budget reconciliation would prevent Republicans from filibustering the legislation, as had been widely expected. Democrats, who currently control 58 seats in the Senate, would be able to pass the measure with a simple majority vote rather than the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster.

Separately, conservative Democrats in the House, who have been pressing for a strong statement from leadership on fiscal responsibility in the budget, may see some of their concerns addressed. A Democratic aide told CNN that House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House Majority Whip Steny Hoyer are drafting a letter to Senate leaders “throwing down the gauntlet” and insisting that a pay-as-you-go system be followed. Such a system would require new federal spending to be offset by budget cuts or tax increases.

President Barack Obama called for the so-called “PAYGO” legislation in his weekend radio address.

According to Conrad, the budget resolution would limit increases in non-defense discretionary spending to 2.9 percent through 2014.

“While the budget resolution takes important steps in the near-term of cutting the deficit in half by 2012 and by two-thirds by 2014, it is clear that more will be needed to address the long-term fiscal imbalance confronting the nation beyond the five-year budget window,” Conrad said.

President Obama gathered his Cabinet members last week and challenged them to identify a total of $100 million in cuts over the next 90 days. Critics said that, in the context of the federal budget, $100 million in savings is a tiny amount. By one comparison, it is equivalent to a car dealer offering to take $1 off the price of a $36,700 vehicle.

“Any amount of savings is obviously welcome,” Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Kentucky, said at the time. “But [$100 million is] about the average amount we’ll spend every single day just covering the interest on the stimulus package that we passed earlier this year.”

White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs said ordinary Americans would nevertheless appreciate the savings effort.

“Only in Washington, D.C., is $100 million dollars not a lot of money,” Gibbs said. “It is where I’m from. It is where I grew up. And I think it is for hundreds of millions of Americans.”

CNN’s Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Late Monday, Democratic leaders in the House and Senate struck a deal on a 2010 budget resolution that contains major spending priorities for the early Obama administration.

Both chambers could take up the measure as soon as Tuesday. President Obama’s budget proposal totals $3.67 trillion.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Kent Conrad praised the agreement in a statement, calling it “a major accomplishment.” He said the plan advances Obama’s objectives, including cutting U.S. reliance on foreign energy, improving education, changing the health care system, and offering tax relief to the middle class.

The deal was reached while lawmakers were working to merge the separate House and Senate versions of the budget plan. The full House and Senate are expected to vote on the fiscal year 2010 budget resolution during the week, with the House potentially voting as early as Tuesday.

Negotiators have moved quickly on part of the budget procedure. A significant health care overhaul is now expected to win approval this year because Democrats are using a special mechanism called budget reconciliation. That process would prevent Republicans from blocking the bill through a filibuster, a tactic many had anticipated.

Because Democrats hold 58 Senate seats, reconciliation would allow them to pass the legislation with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes normally required to defeat a filibuster.

Meanwhile, some fiscally conservative House Democrats who had sought a stronger commitment to budget discipline may see some of their concerns answered. A Democratic aide told CNN that House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House Majority Whip Steny Hoyer are preparing a letter to Senate leaders that would “throw down the gauntlet” by demanding adherence to a pay-as-you-go approach. Under that system, new federal spending would have to be balanced by either spending reductions or tax hikes.

Obama also urged passage of PAYGO legislation during his weekend radio address.

According to Conrad, the budget resolution would hold growth in non-defense discretionary spending to 2.9 percent through 2014.

Conrad said the measure makes meaningful short-term progress by aiming to cut the deficit in half by 2012 and by two-thirds by 2014. However, he added that further action will be necessary to deal with the country’s longer-term fiscal problems beyond the five-year budget period.

Last week, Obama met with his Cabinet and instructed its members to find a combined $100 million in savings over the next 90 days.

Critics argued that, compared with the overall federal budget, $100 million is very small. One comparison described it as similar to a car dealer reducing the price of a $36,700 vehicle by $1.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, a Kentucky Republican, said at the time that any savings were welcome, but noted that $100 million was roughly equal to what the government would spend each day just on interest payments for the stimulus package passed earlier in the year.

White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs responded that ordinary Americans would still value the effort to save money.

“Only in Washington, D.C., is $100 million dollars not a lot of money,” Gibbs said. “It is where I’m from. It is where I grew up. And I think it is for hundreds of millions of Americans.”

CNN’s Deirdre Walsh contributed to the report.

House and Senate Democrats reached agreement on a fiscal year 2010 budget resolution designed to advance President Barack Obama’s broad domestic agenda, a $3.67 trillion plan that places major emphasis on health care reform, clean energy, education, and tax relief for middle-class families. The agreement represents an important step in moving the administration’s priorities through Congress and gives Democratic leaders a procedural path to pursue some of their most ambitious goals.

A central feature of the deal is the use of budget reconciliation, a parliamentary procedure that allows certain tax and spending measures to pass the Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes normally needed to overcome a filibuster. By including reconciliation instructions, Democrats preserved the option of moving major legislation even if Republicans oppose it as a bloc. This is especially significant for health care reform, one of Obama’s top priorities, because it makes passage more likely by reducing the ability of Senate Republicans to block the bill through extended debate.

The budget resolution does not itself enact new health care, energy, education, or tax policies. Instead, it sets broad spending and revenue targets and creates the framework Congress can use to draft and pass later legislation. Democratic leaders argued that the resolution provides room for investments intended to expand health coverage, reduce dependence on foreign oil, improve schools, and provide tax relief to working families.

At the same time, the agreement attempts to respond to concerns about rising deficits and long-term fiscal discipline. Democrats included support for “pay-as-you-go,” or PAYGO, rules, which generally require new spending increases or tax cuts to be offset by spending reductions or revenue increases elsewhere. Supporters said PAYGO would help ensure that new initiatives do not add unnecessarily to the deficit, while allowing the government to make targeted investments during a period of economic weakness.

The compromise reflects the balancing act facing Democratic lawmakers in 2009: advancing an ambitious agenda after Obama’s election while reassuring moderates and fiscal conservatives that Congress would not ignore the nation’s budget problems. For liberal Democrats, the reconciliation language offered a powerful tool to enact health care reform and other priorities. For more deficit-conscious members, the PAYGO commitment provided a measure of fiscal restraint.

Republicans, however, criticized the budget plan as too costly and warned that reconciliation could be used to force through sweeping policy changes without meaningful bipartisan support. They argued that major reforms, especially in health care, should be debated under normal Senate procedures and should not be protected from a filibuster. Democrats countered that the budget process was necessary to prevent obstruction and to deliver on promises made during the 2008 campaign.

The agreement marked a major legislative victory for Democratic leaders and the Obama administration. By aligning the House and Senate around a single budget framework, Democrats positioned themselves to begin the next phase of work on the president’s domestic agenda. Most notably, the deal increased the likelihood that Congress would be able to pass significant health care reform, a goal that had eluded previous administrations for decades.

**Democrats reach deal on 2010 budget blueprint, preserving path for health care overhaul**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — House and Senate Democrats reached agreement on a fiscal year 2010 budget resolution during President Barack Obama’s first year in office, setting up a broad governing blueprint that included room for health care reform, new fiscal discipline rules and the possible use of a fast-track congressional procedure to move major legislation through the Senate.

The agreement, negotiated by Democratic leaders and budget committee chairs, was designed to align Congress with key elements of Obama’s domestic agenda while also responding to concerns among moderate Democrats about rising deficits following the financial crisis and federal rescue efforts.

The budget resolution was not a law and did not require the president’s signature, but it served as Congress’ fiscal framework for the year. Most significantly, it included language allowing Democrats to use **budget reconciliation** for health care legislation — a procedural tool that could allow certain budget-related provisions to pass the Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes typically needed to overcome a filibuster.

Democrats said reconciliation was a fallback option, not their preferred route.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman **Kent Conrad**, a North Dakota Democrat and fiscal hawk, emphasized that the agreement did not mean Democrats were abandoning bipartisan negotiations on health care. Conrad had been wary of using reconciliation for sweeping policy changes, but he said the budget preserved the option in case Republicans refused to engage on a serious health care package.

Conrad and other Democrats also highlighted the inclusion of **PAYGO**, or “pay-as-you-go,” budget rules. PAYGO generally requires that new tax cuts or entitlement spending be offset by savings or revenue increases elsewhere, a principle Democrats said was necessary to restore discipline after years of deficit spending.

The budget agreement called for reducing the deficit over time while still making room for Obama’s priorities, including health care reform, energy policy, education investments and tax relief aimed at middle-class families.

Republicans sharply criticized the deal, arguing that Democrats were preparing to push through an expensive and partisan agenda at a time of mounting federal debt.

Senate Republican Leader **Mitch McConnell** of Kentucky said the reconciliation language showed Democrats were willing to sidestep the minority party and “jam” through a health care bill without broad support. Republicans argued that using reconciliation for health care would undermine Senate tradition and limit debate on one of the largest domestic policy changes in decades.

The White House defended the agreement as a responsible step toward advancing Obama’s agenda while addressing long-term fiscal challenges.

White House press secretary **Robert Gibbs** said the administration was pleased that congressional Democrats had produced a budget consistent with the president’s priorities. Gibbs said the framework kept health care reform moving forward, supported middle-class tax relief and embraced PAYGO as part of a commitment to fiscal responsibility.

Health care reform was the central political issue embedded in the budget fight. Obama had made expanding coverage and lowering health care costs a top priority, and Democratic leaders wanted to ensure they had every procedural option available if bipartisan talks stalled.

Under reconciliation, legislation is protected from a Senate filibuster and debate time is limited. However, the process is constrained by Senate rules requiring provisions to have a direct budgetary impact, meaning not every element of a health care overhaul could necessarily be included.

The agreement reflected the difficult balance Democrats faced in 2009: moving quickly on Obama’s ambitious domestic program while reassuring voters and moderate lawmakers that the party was not ignoring the deficit.

The budget resolution was expected to clear both chambers with Democratic support, though few, if any, Republicans were expected to vote for it.

**WASHINGTON —** Congressional Democrats moved Tuesday to put the finishing touches on a fiscal 2010 budget blueprint built around President Barack Obama’s $3.67 trillion spending plan, setting up a debate over taxes, health care, energy policy and the government’s long-term deficit outlook.

The budget resolution, being readied by Democratic leaders in the House and Senate, would not have the force of law, but it would establish the framework for later tax and spending legislation. It also could include instructions allowing Democrats to use the fast-track budget reconciliation process for major pieces of Obama’s agenda, potentially enabling them to pass legislation with a simple Senate majority and avoid a Republican filibuster.

Democratic leaders said the plan reflects the administration’s priorities: reviving the economy, expanding health care coverage, investing in clean energy and education, and beginning to reduce deficits once the recession eases.

“We are writing a budget that meets the crisis we inherited and lays the foundation for long-term growth,” one senior Democratic lawmaker said. “The American people expect us to act on jobs, health care and energy, and this resolution gives us the tools to do that.”

Republicans sharply criticized the proposal, arguing that it would lock in excessive spending, raise taxes and add to the national debt at a time when federal deficits are already soaring because of the recession and the financial rescue effort.

“This budget spends too much, taxes too much and borrows too much,” a Republican budget committee member said. “Families are tightening their belts, but Washington is preparing to spend trillions more.”

The Obama budget projects a deficit of more than $1 trillion in the near term, reflecting the economic downturn, lower tax receipts and emergency spending to stabilize the economy. Democrats contend that the deficit will shrink in later years as the economy recovers and as the administration seeks savings in areas such as Medicare payments, agricultural subsidies and certain tax preferences.

Still, deficit reduction remains a central point of contention. Moderate Democrats have pressed leaders to show a credible path toward bringing annual deficits down as a share of the economy, warning that financial markets and voters could lose patience with open-ended borrowing.

“We can support bold investments, but we also have to demonstrate fiscal discipline,” a centrist Democrat said. “A budget that does not address the deficit will not be sustainable politically or economically.”

The most sensitive procedural issue is reconciliation. Democratic leaders have considered using it as a backstop for health care reform and possibly changes to student lending or energy policy. Reconciliation bills cannot be filibustered in the Senate, making the process attractive in a chamber where Democrats face unified Republican opposition and may struggle to assemble 60 votes.

But the tactic carries political risks. Republicans say using reconciliation for major policy changes would amount to ramming through partisan legislation. Some Democrats, particularly in the Senate, are also wary of relying too heavily on the process, arguing that sweeping health care changes should be bipartisan if possible.

“We would prefer to move major legislation through regular order,” a Democratic senator said. “But we are not going to give the minority a veto over the president’s agenda.”

The House and Senate budget plans are expected to differ in details, including the level of discretionary spending, assumptions about tax policy, and the scope of reconciliation instructions. Those differences would have to be resolved in a conference agreement before Congress adopts a final budget resolution.

The resolution is likely to preserve Obama’s call to extend middle-class tax cuts while allowing tax reductions for wealthier households enacted under President George W. Bush to expire. It also assumes revenue from proposals aimed at limiting certain deductions for high-income taxpayers, though some Democrats have expressed reservations about those provisions.

On health care, Democrats say the budget will create room for legislation aimed at expanding coverage and restraining costs, but it will not settle the specifics. The administration has argued that health care reform is essential to long-term deficit reduction because federal spending on Medicare and Medicaid is one of the biggest drivers of future debt.

“Getting health care costs under control is deficit reduction,” a House Democrat involved in the budget talks said. “If we do nothing, the budget problem only gets worse.”

Republicans counter that Democrats are using deficit concerns to justify a large expansion of government. They say Congress should focus instead on spending restraints, entitlement reform and tax policies designed to encourage private investment.

The coming budget votes will offer an early test of Obama’s ability to keep Democrats united behind his economic program. With large Democratic majorities in both chambers, the resolution is expected to pass, but defections from fiscal conservatives could complicate the process and force leaders to adjust spending or deficit targets.

For now, Democratic leaders are presenting the budget as both a response to the recession and a statement of governing priorities.

“This is not just a ledger,” one leadership aide said. “It is a roadmap for the country we are trying to build.”

**Democrats Reach Budget Deal, Clearing Path for Obama Priorities**  
*April 2009*

WASHINGTON — House and Senate Democrats have reached agreement on a congressional budget blueprint that embraces much of President Obama’s domestic agenda, including major investments in health care, education and clean energy, while setting the stage for a high-stakes fight over health care reform later this year.

The deal, negotiated by Democratic leaders from both chambers, is not a binding spending law but serves as a broad fiscal roadmap for Congress. It allows Democrats to move forward on several of Obama’s top priorities while attempting to answer Republican criticism that the new administration is dramatically expanding the size and cost of government.

A key feature of the agreement is its treatment of health care reform. The budget deal preserves the possibility of using a fast-track parliamentary procedure known as reconciliation, which would allow Democrats to pass health care legislation in the Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes normally needed to overcome a filibuster. Democratic leaders have said they prefer a bipartisan health care bill, but keeping reconciliation available gives them leverage if negotiations with Republicans stall.

The budget framework also broadly supports Obama’s proposals to expand access to health insurance, invest in renewable energy, and make college more affordable. At the same time, it trims some of the president’s requested spending levels, reflecting concerns among moderate Democrats about rising deficits.

One of the compromises in the agreement involves limits on non-defense discretionary spending. Congressional Democrats agreed to hold those programs to lower levels than Obama had originally sought, a move intended to show fiscal restraint while still protecting domestic initiatives central to the president’s agenda. Defense spending and major entitlement programs such as Medicare and Social Security are treated separately from those caps.

Republicans, however, dismissed the budget deal as a vehicle for higher taxes, more spending and deeper debt. They argued that Democrats were using the economic crisis to justify a long-term expansion of federal programs. GOP lawmakers also criticized the potential use of reconciliation for health care, saying it would allow Democrats to push through sweeping policy changes without meaningful bipartisan support.

The agreement comes as the Obama administration is trying to balance an ambitious policy agenda with growing public concern over deficits following the financial bailout and economic stimulus package.

That tension was underscored by Obama’s recent directive asking Cabinet agencies to identify a combined $100 million in administrative savings. The White House presented the effort as a symbolic step toward eliminating waste and changing Washington’s spending habits.

But critics from both parties noted that $100 million is minuscule compared with a federal budget measured in trillions of dollars. Republicans mocked the savings goal as a public-relations gesture, while some budget analysts said it would do little to affect the deficit.

White House officials countered that the Cabinet savings push was not intended to solve the fiscal problem on its own, but to signal that agencies must scrutinize even small expenses as Congress considers much larger budget decisions.

The budget deal now positions Democrats to move ahead with Obama’s legislative agenda, but the hardest fights remain unresolved. Health care reform, in particular, is expected to dominate the coming months, testing Democratic unity and the administration’s ability to turn a campaign promise into law.

The budget agreement also reflects Obama’s broader priorities, including investments in energy, education and health care, while setting the terms for future congressional action on taxes and spending.

Republicans have criticized the reconciliation option, arguing it would limit debate and allow Democrats to pass sweeping policy changes with a narrow partisan majority. Democrats counter that the procedure has been used by both parties in the past and say urgent action is needed to address rising health care costs and expand coverage.

If the House and Senate approve the budget resolution, lawmakers could begin using reconciliation later in the year to move health care-related provisions that directly affect federal spending or revenues.

— With reporting from CNN’s Deirdre Walsh.
